subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: I share a flat with Lokesh, so I saw this play out. Two weeks ago at the college canteen a senior kept mocking Pooja's stammer while about ten people laughed or looked away. Lokesh was there and said nothing; I know because Lokesh told me that night, sitting on the balcony staring at the street. Lokesh was quiet for days. Then on Friday Lokesh went and found Pooja and said, "I saw what happened and I did nothing. I am sorry." Pooja shrugged, said thanks, and then told Lokesh what it had felt like. I stood at the door. I think it cost Lokesh a lot to say it. Lokesh has already decided that next time it will be sitting beside Pooja straight away.

qa.q: What did the senior do at the college canteen?
qa.a: A senior kept mocking Pooja's stammer at the college canteen while about ten people laughed or looked away.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling during the days after the canteen?
qa.a: Lokesh felt regret and shame, staring at the street and staying quiet for days, which turned into a wish to apologise.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do with the shame instead of hiding it?
qa.a: Lokesh went to Pooja, admitted watching and doing nothing, apologised, and decided to sit beside Pooja next time.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Pooja to hear Lokesh's apology and then describe how it had felt?
qa.a: Pooja probably felt some relief at being seen and believed; shrugging and saying thanks before opening up suggests careful trust.

grounding: A young adult regrets watching and doing nothing, uses the shame to decide how to act next time and apologises to the person affected.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Monday. In the hostel lounge four people laughed as someone filmed Tushar tripping and spilling his tea, and no one helped. Ayesha stood at the doorway with her books, telling herself it was just a joke. Tushar left without a word. Tuesday. Ayesha could not concentrate. The picture of Tushar walking out kept replaying, and shame settled in her chest. Thursday. Ayesha knocked on Tushar's door. "I watched on Monday and did nothing, and I am sorry. If it happens again I will come over to you at once." Tushar looked surprised, then said, "Thanks for saying so." They sat and drank tea.

qa.q: What did Ayesha say when knocking on Tushar's door?
qa.a: Ayesha said, "I watched on Monday and did nothing, and I am sorry."

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling on Tuesday?
qa.a: Ayesha felt shame and guilt, unable to concentrate as the picture of Tushar walking out kept replaying.

qa.q: What turning point on Thursday moved Ayesha from shame to action?
qa.a: Ayesha knocked on Tushar's door, apologised for watching and promised to come over at once next time.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt when Ayesha knocked and apologised?
qa.a: Tushar probably felt surprised and a little comforted to learn that one person had noticed and cared; the thanks and the shared tea suggest relief.

grounding: A young adult regrets having watched and done nothing, and apologises to the person affected while deciding how to act next time.
